Comorbid Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease and Stiff Person 
Syndrome: A Case Report (P4.322) 
Matthew Lustig, Shaena Blevins 
First published April 4, 2016,

 Info & Disclosures 
Abstract 
Objective: To report a rare case of comorbid Idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (IPD) and Stiff 
Person Syndrome (SPS). Background: Although IPD and SPS may have similar clinical 
presentations, the much higher prevalence of IPD makes SPS less likely to be suspected. 
Management options are different enough for IPD and SPS that failure to respond to treatment for 
IPD may increase suspicion of SPS (and vice versa). This is a case of a patient whose diagnosis 
was changed from IPD to SPS, and then back-and-forth many times (from many different 
neurologists) until, ultimately, the diagnoses of comorbid IPD and SPS were made. Case: A 67-
year-old Caucasian male presented 7 years ago with gradual onset bilateral lower extremity 
muscle spasms and rigidity. He initially responded to a trial of carbidopa/levodopa, and the 
diagnosis of IPD was made. However, his symptoms gradually returned, with temporary relief 
provided by dopamine agonists and benztropine. His incomplete response to dopamine, his lack 
of upper extremity involvement, and his absence of tremor or freezing raised the possibility of 
SPS. An SPS panel revealed strongly positive anti-GAD antibody titers (>250:1); however, a 
paraneoplastic antibody panel and neoplastic screening exam were negative. He had minimal 
response to IVIG, but plasma exchange resulted in drastic improvement. With time, however, he 
stopped responding to plasma exchange. Diazepam and an intrathecal baclofen trial were 
beneficial, but less beneficial than resuming dopamine agonists and carbidopa/levodopa. A 
DaTscan was positive, and bilateral GPi deep brain stimulators were implanted in order to 
manage the rigidity associated with both IPD and SPS. Current management continues to 
improve rigidity and painful leg spasms; however, he is now wheelchair-bound due to extreme 
freezing and postural instability. Conclusion: Although SPS should be in the differential for IPD 
(and vice versa), their comorbidity should not be discounted. 
Disclosure: Dr. Lustig has nothing to disclose. Dr. Blevins has nothing to disclose.
